package_info.why_malicious: The mod_sed module contains a buffer mishandling vulnerability (CVE-2022-23943) that allows attackers to trigger an out-of-bounds write by sending large request or response bodies, leading to Denial of Service (DoS) and potentially Remote Code Execution (RCE) in non-default configurations where mod_sed is used as an input or output filter.

execution_context.file_location: httpd.conf or any Apache configuration file (e.g., <Directory> directive)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<Directory />
  AllowOverride none
  Require all denied
  AddInputFilter Sed html
  InputSed "s/\(.*\)/Z/g"
</Directory>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At configuration-time, the server is set to process all HTML requests' bodies with mod_sed, which manipulates the request body using a sed expression.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Enabling mod_sed as an input filter on untrusted client data exposes the server to buffer mishandling vulnerabilities.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal configurations do not use mod_sed to process large, untrusted client data; this increases attack surface.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: mod_sed can be legitimately used for stream editing in controlled environments.
key_indicators: InputSed directive processing arbitrary request bodies

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when processing large request or response bodies, the function miscalculates buffer size and performs an out-of-bounds write with memcpy, leading to process crash or potential code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of signed int for buffer size calculations allows integer overflows, enabling attackers to trigger out-of-bounds writes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Buffer management should use safe, unsigned types and validate input sizes; this code fails to do so.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Buffer appending is common, but must be done with proper bounds checking.
key_indicators: buffer size calculation using signed int

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, if a buffer remains after processing, it is appended to the line buffer without sufficient size checks, potentially triggering the vulnerability with large input.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly appending large, untrusted buffers without robust size checks is unsafe.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal code should validate buffer sizes before appending.
key_indicators: appendmem_to_linebuf called with large, unchecked buffer

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, during stream finalization, the code appends a null terminator to the buffer, which can trigger the vulnerability if the buffer is already at or near its maximum size.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Appending to a potentially full buffer without size validation can cause overflows.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Finalization routines should always check buffer capacity before writing.
key_indicators: append_to_linebuf called without buffer size check
potential for off-by-one or overflow errors

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a large (2GB or 4GB) HTTP request body to an endpoint with mod_sed input filter enabled.
attack_chain.leads_to: mod_sed processes the large, untrusted input.

attack_chain.action: mod_sed attempts to append the large buffer to its internal line buffer using appendmem_to_linebuf.
attack_chain.leads_to: Buffer size miscalculation and potential out-of-bounds write.

attack_chain.action: During stream finalization, mod_sed appends a null terminator, which can also trigger the vulnerability if the buffer is full.
attack_chain.leads_to: Process crash (DoS) or, in rare cases, potential code execution.

behavioral_signatures: mod_sed input or output filter enabled on routes processing large request/response bodies
Apache process crashes after receiving large POST requests
Unusually large memory allocations or memcpy operations in mod_sed
file_indicators: Presence of mod_sed in loaded modules
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests with body sizes near 2GB or 4GB
Repeated large requests to endpoints with mod_sed filters
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Apache configuration files for AddInputFilter or AddOutputFilter directives using mod_sed. Watch for large HTTP request bodies (near 2GB or 4GB) and correlate with Apache process crashes or restarts. Use memory safety tools to detect out-of-bounds writes in mod_sed. Automated scanners should flag any use of mod_sed input filters on routes accepting untrusted data.
